extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers seeking norms for composing and judging poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative criteria for composing and evaluating poetry (Renaissance poetics): standards about the poet's purpose, form, effects on readers, and the moral/educational functions of different poetic kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's defining note: feigning notable images with delightful teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is defined as 'feigning notable images of virtues, vices, or what else, with that delightful teaching' and uses verse as his 'fittest raiment'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should combine imagination (feigning) with instruction (teaching) and delight. The manner should not be 'table-talk' or loose speech, but composed: 'piecing each syllable of each word by just proportion, according to the dignity of the subject.' The poet must form images that both please and instruct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final end of learning: lead to virtuous action
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of learning (and therefore of poetry as a learning-instrument) is 'to lead and draw us to as high a perfection as our degenerate souls ... can be capable of' — i.e., to virtue and right action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry by whether it purifies wit, enriches memory, enables judgment, and enlarges conceit in ways that incline readers toward virtuous practice rather than mere knowledge. Poetry's highest merit is its contribution to moral action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should combine precept and example (surpass philosopher and historian)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet performs both what the philosopher (precept/general) and the historian (example/particular) do: he couples the general notion with a particular example — 'a perfect picture'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem supplies both the universal rule and a vivid particular instance that makes the rule graspable and memorable. Philosophical abstraction alone is too obscure; history's mere particulars are not sufficiently doctrinal. Great poetry unites both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell: vivid imagery that 'strikes, pierces, and possesses' the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'yieldeth to the powers of the mind an image' which better illuminates the imagination than philosophers' verbal definitions. A spoken picture (painting, model) helps comprehension more than abstract description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate success by the liveliness and concreteness of images: do they enable readers to 'see' the quality (anger, courage, remorse) rather than merely read a definition? Examples: theatrical depictions (Ajax, Œdipus) that make passions visible and intelligible to all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry treats the universal (what ought to be) rather than mere particular facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Aristotle, poetry is 'more philosophical' because it deals with the universal consideration (what is fit to be said or done), whereas history deals with the particular (what actually was).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetry on whether it captures general truths or lessons that guide action, not simply on factual accuracy. For moral instruction, a well-framed feigned example can be more useful than a strict factual report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet may craft feigned examples for better teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets can fabricate or adapt examples (feign) to illustrate the most reasonable course of action and to teach without the contingencies or harms of strict history — e.g., learning stratagems from Xenophon’s feigned Abradatus rather than a harsher factual model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poet's invented scenarios are plausible and tuned to instruct and move readers; a feigned example is permissible and often preferable if it better reveals causes, morals, and apt conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary virtue of poetry: to move readers to practice (praxis), not merely teach knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement (being moved to act) is of a higher order than mere knowledge; poetry should excite desire to be taught and to act: 'who will be taught, if he be not moved with desire to be taught?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a poem not only imparts doctrines but also inspires readers to enact them. Poems that leave readers intellectually informed but unmoved are deficient in moral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and delight: use of musicality, tale, and pleasurable form to entice readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'cometh to you with words set in delightful proportion, either accompanied with, or prepared for, the well-enchanting skill of music; and with a tale' — using pleasure to attract even those resistant to moral instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the poem’s formal qualities (rhythm, diction, narrative) by how well they enthrall readers of varied capacities (children, old men, 'tenderest stomachs') so that moral lessons penetrate through delight rather than didactic fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should present virtue attractively and vice dissuasively
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'sets virtue so out in her best colours' and makes vice appear manacled or contemptible, thereby encouraging imitation of the good and discouragement of evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poem frames virtuous actions as admirable and desirable (fortune made a handmaid to virtue on stage) and whether it renders vice unattractive or punished so as to dissuade imitation — avoiding depictions that unintentionally celebrate vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess poetry by both its works (whole) and its parts (kinds/genres)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should 'weight this latter sort of poetry by his works, and then by his parts' — evaluate both the totality of a poet’s achievement and the quality of individual parts (genres, modes, mixed forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical evaluation should include overall effect and the merits/defects of component parts (style, plot, character, meter, genre-mixing). Mixtures of kinds (tragical and comical, prose and verse) are acceptable if the constituent parts are well executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral: small forms that can teach about social wrongs and contentment
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastoral poems (e.g., Melibæus, Tityrus) can show 'the misery of people under hard lords' or 'the blessedness derived to them that lie lowest from the goodness of them that sit highest', and thus dramatize wrong-doing and patience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge pastorals on their capacity to encode social and moral lessons behind simple rural speech and images. Even light or 'poor' pipes may move hearts and reveal justice or injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegiac: move pity and point out human weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Lamenting elegies 'in a kind heart, would move rather pity than blame' and accompany lamentation with compassion or correct emphasis on human wretchedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate elegies on their capacity to arouse sympathetic reflection and to direct mourning towards moral insight rather than mere sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iambic (satirical bite): expose vice and provoke shame
rubrics_metrics.description: The iambic 'rubs the galled mind, making shame the trumpet of villany' — it openly cries out against naughtiness and uses sharpness to correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess iambic or biting verse by its effectiveness in shaming vice without mere cruelty and in prompting reform through satire's sting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: amusing exposure that induces self-recognition and shame
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire 'Omne vafer vitium ridenti tangit amico' — sportingly makes men laugh at folly and, ultimately, ashamed of it, by touching vices in a friendly laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge satire by its balance of wit and correction: does it expose folly in a way that leads the reader to laugh at themselves and so desist from vice, rather than merely ridicule or defame?

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: imitation of common errors to teach by ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates 'the common errors of our life' in the most ridiculous manner so that 'it is impossible that any beholder can be content to be such a one.' It furnishes recognizable signifying badges of vice (niggardly Demea, crafty Davus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comedy on whether it successfully shows everyday vices so as to produce corrective self-awareness; it must make faults so contemptible that audiences abstain from them rather than learn to admire them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: moves admiration and pity, shows uncertainty and moral lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy 'openeth the greatest wounds' and by stirring admiration and commiseration teaches 'the uncertainty of this world' and how fragile gilded foundations are; it can soften even hardened hearts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tragic works by their capacity to move pity and fear (Aristotelian catharsis), to reveal moral lessons about pride, ambition, and the transience of fortune, and to effect inward change in the spectator (e.g., Plutarch’s account of Alexander Pheræus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric: praise of virtue and raising courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyric poetry with 'tuned lyre and well-accorded voice' gives praise (the reward of virtue), moral precepts, and can raise thought and courage (example: old songs of Percy and Douglas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge lyric poems on their ability to ennoble listeners, praise virtuous deeds effectively, and stir collective courage and honorable enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroical: the highest kind, instructs in magnanimity and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroical poem 'teacheth and moveth to the most high and excellent truth' and sets lofty examples (Achilles, Cyrus, Æneas) that 'inform with counsel how to be worthy' across many situations (war, peace, governance, inward life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate heroic poetry as the most consequential kind: does it present models of magnanimity and justice in a sustained, illustrative way that can shape a reader’s conduct and ideals?

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confining moral instruction to abstruse forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers often teach 'obscurely' so only the learned understand; poetry should be accessible — 'the poet is the food for the tenderest stomachs' and 'the right popular philosopher.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether poetry communicates moral instruction to non-specialists without sacrificing depth: clarity, narrative, and affective force are virtues when the aim is broad moral formation.
